searchText: Because people who read the repos are not that nuanced. Separating clearly what is automated and what is manual is helpful for readers of the system. It is valuable enough information to have its own status. To make a user drill in to get the nuanced difference is not helpful. We could have every status be a subfield but we don’t. The reason we don’t is because it is a communication device to the readers of the repo. Cognitively the difference between, this concept got here because no one pushed it forward, and it got here because of the explicit request of the author is valuable information. Burying this into a field for more information is further to get that information. Functionally if we went your way we will have a huge list of many withdrawns. And most of them will be “due to inactivity” To find ones that were actually withdrawn by the author not an editor people would need to comb the list to find them. Again, there is a big difference between the ball was dropped and the someone actively withdrew an EIP. Will you force everyone to write a reasoning? Is that going to be a required field? Should we make them give a reasoning just so we can have editors be able to move things to withdrawn? > To find ones that were actually withdrawn by the author not an editor people would need to comb the list to find them. What is the user story for someone looking for this list? The user stories I have in mind are: * People building stuff looking for an appropriate standard to follow * People looking at a specific EIP (by number or by link) 1) I look through the list of Stagnant EIPs to see what ideas are their but didn’t get pushed forward. 2) look through the list to find which ones were actively withdrawn. For example block rewards funding. It is a clear signal to the community why an EIP is the status it is. These are the people I have in mind when trying to design things, and neither care about being able to browse withdrawn/stagnant/abandoned EIPs. We keep them so links continue to work, but we don't need them in a readily available list. Which is valuable, particularly among contentious EIPs. Do you think users who aren't familiar with the EIP process are doing that? That is, people who don't understand what the statuses mean. The community is also an important factor to consider. > Do you think users who aren't familiar with the EIP process are doing that? That is, people who don't understand what the statuses mean. <@301186049323958275> Absolutely, that is part of how progpow escalated when it didn’t need to. What do you mean how ProgPoW escalated when it didn't need to? People read the repo and make assumptions not based on a deep knowledge of the system. People read Accepted and assume it meant something it didn’t. I don't think people were reading EIPs in general, they got a link on Twitter telling them to brigade EIP-XXX. They saw the status. I agree with your view on accepted being bad due to how it signals, I disagree that the same problem will occur with withdrawn. Can you describe a user story for someone confused by withdrawn? How does that turn into a brigading or political problem? Yep, let me write it out (stepping away for a bit, will read after I get back so take your time 🙂) Continuing in the Progpow example. Say that it moved to withdrawn. Opponents of the EIP would jump on that it is Withdrawn and politicize that move. Saying “it is no longer considered” which is not true if it is moved solely because of Inactivity. But, they won’t get the nuance and they won’t care too. The community then will be confused if someone brings it back to draft again. Sighting “why bring it it back? it was withdrawn! Don’t you know what that means” Particularly for contentious EIPs this distinction is important for the community. We will have contentious EIPs again. To avoid confusion all we need is for them to be separated so it is clear from the statuses language itself. I recall Hudson was talking about a "stagnant" explanation to combat that Yes, this is what we discussed over the many calls. Stagnant clearly labels why the EIP is in its status. Without requiring readers to drill in deeper to get context. For withdrawn EIPs, great add the field. The community doesn’t read EIP-1 and live and breath what each status means and why. They just don’t. The EIP process is complex and most don’t understand it at all. We can make this easier for the community at large with the addition of one status that clearly differentiates what is automatic and what is deliberate by an author. That adds a lot of value. Enough value to warrant its own status. Sure, I get this may seem superfluous from an engineering perspective, but from a community management perspective it is a big win for this content to be easily digestible without requiring reading and understanding nuance tied to the process itself. Another example. EFI vs CFI. The eligible made it sound like it was eligible for main net. People thought the list of EFI meant eligible for Berlin. This is false. But it didn’t matter. I instead had to explain the nuance. Why make the added effort of explaining the nuance and give space for confusion when instead we can change the name to “Considered for Inclusion” “Considered” readily explains its state without any further explanation. People that read it get it immediately. No further reading necessary. Status should also be this clear. By creating a subfield that gives a very different reason why an EIP is there gives space for confusion. It’s not worth it. “It was withdrawn. Well who withdrew it? The editors? Why did the editor withdraw it? Oh the editor moved it to withdrawn with the special field for inactivity. Oh, the author didn’t withdraw it, it reached an inactivity limit.” Vs This EIP is Stagnant. Very clear what that means. This EIP was Withdrawn. Explaining, “well the WITHDRAWN EIP isn’t withdrawn technically, the author still may be interested, but this field here tells you that an editor marked the EIP because of inactivity. It isn’t withdrawn it is just in the WITHDRAWN status.” From a community perspective it is too much, when the alternative is to have clearly understood statuses from the language itself that doesn’t require special knowledge about the EIP process to decipher the difference. If we optimized for engineers we wouldn’t need names for the statuses, we could have numbers with definitions. Let’s optimize for anyone who reads a status to understand clearly what it means. It is better for the community. Thanks for the explanation of your position <@!187490121698770945>! I think our differences are sourced in a couple of places. I'm dubious that someone who doesn't understand what `Withdrawn by author` and `Withdrawn due to inactivity` means will understand what `Stagnant` and `Withdrawn` means. I believe that the former two are significantly more verbose/descriptive and *more likely* to result in the outcome you desire than your proposed solution. Perhaps the issue is that you are imagining those two fields showing up separately on the EIPs page, rather than combined? This is what I had in mind for the status field with reason field embedded: The other aspect is that I dislike optimizing our process around people who abuse the process. I would rather deal with those people more directly by redirecting them elsewhere, deleting comments, banning from organization, etc. rather than spoiling our process because they refuse to take a moment to understand it (after having it explained). I get the impression from the above that you are hoping that this change will make it so we (editors) have to moderate less, but I personally believe that there will *always* be some amount of moderation that is necessary no matter how hard we try to make the process intuitive to the casual viewer and at some point we need to stop optimizing for the lowest common denominator and instead favor optimizing for people who appropriately use the system. To me, your proposal for separate statuses crosses that line, though I can appreciate that we disagree on where that line is. <@!425279588009246720> in case you don't get notifications for comments on merged PRs: <https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/2918#issuecomment-691408774> <@!425279588009246720> and <@!543900561460822016> can you two review <https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/2947> when you get the chance? I don't want to mark it as Ready for Review until we are ready to merge because doing so is likely to trigger the auto-merge bot spamming a whole bunch of people. I redid the whole thing, so all previous comments should be made again in case I made the same mistakes again (though I tried to take all previous feedback into consideration, so the same mistakes *shouldn't* be present).

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content:
Thanks for the explanation of your position <@!187490121698770945>!  I think our differences are sourced in a couple of places.

I'm dubious that someone who doesn't understand what `Withdrawn by author` and `Withdrawn due to inactivity` means will understand what `Stagnant` and `Withdrawn` means.  I believe that the former two are significantly more verbose/descriptive and *more likely* to result in the outcome you desire than your proposed solution.  Perhaps the issue is that you are imagining those two fields showing up separately on the EIPs page, rather than combined?  This is what I had in mind for the status field with reason field embedded:

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: The other aspect is that I dislike optimizing our process around people who abuse the process.  I would rather deal with those people more directly by redirecting them elsewhere, deleting comments, banning from organization, etc. rather than spoiling our process because they refuse to take a moment to understand it (after having it explained).  I get the impression from the above that you are hoping that this change will make it so we (editors) have to moderate less, but I personally believe that there will *always* be some amount of moderation that is necessary no matter how hard we try to make the process intuitive to the casual viewer and at some point we need to stop optimizing for the lowest common denominator and instead favor optimizing for people who appropriately use the system.  To me, your proposal for separate statuses crosses that line, though I can appreciate that we disagree on where that line is.
